19 The force–extension graph for a spring is shown.
force
0
0
extension
What represents the work done to extend the spring?
A
the area under the graph
B
the gradient of the graph
C
the reciprocal of the gradient of the graph
D
twice the area under the graph

hints: Notice the axes are force on the y-axis and extension on the x-axis, with a straight line from the origin showing force increasing as the spring stretches.
Recall that work done is force multiplied by distance moved in the direction of the force, so for a varying force you must sum $F \times \Delta x$ strips.
Compare what area and what gradient mean here: check the unit of $\text{N} \times \text{m}$ for area against the unit of $\text{N m}^{-1}$ for gradient.
walkthrough: Identify the graph: force plotted against extension, starting at 0,0 with force proportional to extension, so $F = kx$.
State the physics rule: work done by a varying force equals the sum of small $F \Delta x$ elements, which is the area under the $F$ against $x$ graph.
For this triangular area, work $W = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, with unit $\text{N m} = \text{J}$.
Check the other quantities: gradient $= F/x = k$ and reciprocal of gradient $= 1/k$, neither of which has the unit of energy.
Therefore the work done to extend the spring is represented by the area under the graph. This is option A.

A.explanation: The area under the force-extension line equals $\frac{1}{2}Fx$, which is the elastic potential energy stored and equal to the work done to extend the spring.

B.explanation: The gradient $F/x$ gives the spring constant $k$ in $\text{N m}^{-1}$, not an energy in joules.

C.explanation: The reciprocal of the gradient $x/F$ gives $1/k$, the extension per unit force, not work done.

D.explanation: Twice the triangular area equals $Fx$, which would apply only if the full final force acted over the whole extension, whereas the force builds up from zero.
